# Capturing disaggregated vLLM: NIXL KV over RDMA

Status: built, behind `webhook.nixlPause.enabled` (off by default). Code: `internal/agent/gpushare_nixl.go`, `internal/webhook/gpushare.go`. Needs a node bundle whose GPU tool has `nixl-pause` and `nixl-resume`. Phase 1 of #3551 covers vLLM only.

## The problem

A disaggregated vLLM engine (prefill or decode) whose KV connector is `NixlConnector` over RDMA holds RDMA device files and mappings, memory registrations, and queue pairs to its peers. CRIU cannot dump them (checkpoint-restore/criu#267), so the capture preflight refuses such a pod and its replicas start cold. vLLM has no call that releases the connector and brings it back.

## What it does

The GPU tool runs two operations inside the vLLM processes, through the gpushare library's control socket:

- `nixl-pause`:
  1. The engine stops taking new requests.
  2. It waits up to 60 s for KV transfers in flight.
  3. It shuts its connector down on every TP worker.
  4. The tool checks that no RDMA device file is left open or mapped. If one is, or if any step fails, it resumes every process and exits non-zero.
- `nixl-resume [--host IP]`:
  1. The connectors are created again on the same KV memory under a **new engine id**. Peers cache a remote engine by its id, so the restored one must look new to them.
  2. The engine restarts its side-channel listener, at `IP` when given, and takes requests again.

The agent calls them at the same points as ModelExpress's `mx-pause` / `mx-resume` (GPUSHARE.md, "ModelExpress"). There is one difference: **a paused engine serves nothing**, so every resume is checked.

## Opt-in

| Switch | Set by | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| chart `webhook.nixlPause.enabled` (agent flag `--webhook-nixl-pause`) | the cluster operator | `false` | Off: the annotation below is ignored (logged), and such pods are refused as before. The webhook and the agent both check it (below). |
| pod annotation `nvsnap.io/nixl-pause: "true"` | the workload owner | absent | Opts the workload in; removing it opts out. |

With both on, the webhook adds two variables to each GPU container of a pod under the gpushare library, including a pod that already carries the gpushare placement. A value the pod sets itself is kept.

- `NVSNAP_NIXL_PAUSE=1`: the marker in the container's spec that records the opt-in at admission.
- `NVSNAP_GPUSHARE_CTL_ON_CUDA_USE=1`: the library opens its control socket on a process's first CUDA entry-point lookup. vLLM's engine-core process at TP > 1 allocates no GPU memory, and `nixl-pause` reaches the engine through it.

The pod cannot opt itself in by setting `NVSNAP_NIXL_PAUSE=1`: with the switch off, the webhook replaces a value a GPU container of a pod under the library sets itself with `0`, and the agent pauses only when its own `--webhook-nixl-pause` is on, whatever the process's environment says (a value from `envFrom` is not visible at admission). Such a pod is refused by the preflight as before, and the agent logs the marker it ignored. With the switch on, a pod is opted in only when all three hold: the agent's switch, the annotation `nvsnap.io/nixl-pause: "true"`, and `NVSNAP_NIXL_PAUSE=1` as the webhook set it in the container's spec at admission (`nixlOptInFromPod`, `internal/agent/gpushare_nixl.go`). A variable the pod sets itself without the annotation is not an opt-in.

The variables are added after the process configuration is stamped from the pod as submitted (`process_config.go`), so they don't change which checkpoint a pod restores. A change to the switch applies to pods admitted after it.

## Capture

- **Preflight.** For an opted-in pod, the RDMA findings of its GPU processes under the library become information instead of a block. Two cases are refused with the limit named:
  - the pod also loads through ModelExpress: each pause fails while the other still holds RDMA;
  - the engine spans nodes: untested, and its remote workers are released through the engine's own RPC.

  The opt-in is read from the pod, as admitted, not from a process's environment: the agent's switch, the annotation, and `NVSNAP_NIXL_PAUSE=1` in the GPU container's spec (which the webhook sets). vLLM renames its engine and worker processes with `setproctitle`, which overwrites a process's environment and command line in place, so the process holding the RDMA may show no marker. An image's own `ENV NVSNAP_NIXL_PAUSE=1` without the annotation is not an opt-in. A pod that asked for nixl-pause but is not opted in (the switch is off, it was admitted without the env, or it cannot be read) gets a finding saying why, beside the RDMA that blocks it. The limits are read per container: its engine spans nodes when any of its processes carries `NVSNAP_GPUSHARE_FABRIC=1`, a group size above one (`LWS_GROUP_SIZE`, `GROVE_PCSG_TEMPLATE_NUM_PODS`) or a multi-node engine flag, or when the pod's spec says so (`nvsnap.io/gpushare-fabric: "true"`, such a flag, a KubeRay `ray.io/node-type` label, a LeaderWorkerSet size or Grove pod count above one, or a Grove count the webhook cannot read). The flags are those only an engine on several nodes has: `--headless`, `--nnodes` or `--num-nodes` above one, `--node-rank` or `--data-parallel-start-rank` above zero, `--dist-init-addr`, and `--data-parallel-size-local` below `--data-parallel-size` (the leader of a vLLM data-parallel engine that spans nodes). An address alone (`--data-parallel-address`, `--master-addr`) does not count, since single-node engines set them too. A pod annotated `nvsnap.io/gpushare-fabric: "false"` is still refused when its spec or processes show it spans nodes. Every capture applies these limits itself before `nixl-pause`, whether or not a preflight ran (a capture through `POST /v1/checkpoints` runs none): the pod's spec as admitted (`nixlCaptureRefusal` in `internal/agent/gpushare_nixl.go`), then ModelExpress and the processes (`nixlPauseLimit`, from `pauseNIXLFor`). An agent whose switch is on refuses a capture whose pod it cannot read, since the opt-in is then unknown.

  RDMA of any other process still blocks.
- **Capture-time refusal.** The capture checks itself that the engine does not span nodes, before anything is paused. A group capture's driver tells each member on how many nodes the instance's GPU ranks run. More than one is refused, and so is a session whose driver does not say. One GPU rank with its companions (etcd, NATS, a frontend), captured together on one node, is paused. A process of the container that says it spans nodes (as above) is also refused. The instance's preflight applies the same rank-node rule. A capture requested through `POST /v1/checkpoints` runs no preflight.
- **Pause.** Right before the suspend, after the instance is held and the capture claimed, as `mx-pause`, the agent runs `nixl-pause` on the GPU processes. The agent allows 3 minutes. If the tool fails, the capture fails there with the tool's reason, before anything is stopped. The tool resumes the engine on failure, but the agent's timeout could stop it first, so the agent also runs `nixl-resume`; on an engine that is not paused it answers `not paused`. If that resume fails too, the source is replaced. A deadline that stops the tool does not stop the pause inside the engine. The library serves its control socket one request at a time, so the agent's `nixl-resume` reaches each process only once that process's pause has finished or rolled itself back. It then undoes the pause, or answers `not paused`. A resume that gets no answer within the tool's 120 s per reply fails, and the source is replaced.
  - The usual refusal is NCCL at TP > 1 in a pod with RDMA NICs: NCCL opens the RDMA devices even within one node and keeps them open until the process exits. The tool does not count NCCL's RDMA when NCCL takes its verbs from the bundled `libnvsnap_ibv.so` (chart `webhook.gpushareIBV` or pod annotation `nvsnap.io/gpushare-ibv`, GPUSHARE.md "NCCL over InfiniBand or RoCE"), which releases it at the GPU suspend. That combination has not been run with a NIXL KV engine yet.
  - Neither nvsnap nor this document suggests changing the workload's transport to get around a refusal.
- **No connector.** A pod that opted in but has no NIXL KV connector answers `ok no NIXL KV connector`, and captures as before. The pause and the resume address only the processes whose library has its control socket open (`@nvsnap-gpushare.<pid>` in the pod's network namespace). A process under the library that never used CUDA (a resource tracker, a shell wrapper) has none: the tool cannot reach it and prints nothing for it. Among the processes addressed, only `ok no ...` from every one counts as nothing paused. Output the agent cannot read, or a process that did not answer, counts as paused: the source is resumed when it runs on, and the checkpoint records the pause. A resume succeeds only when every process addressed answered `ok`, and fails when no process has a socket.
- **Rollback.** On every path where the source runs on (a failed capture after the pause, a leave-running dump), the agent runs `nixl-resume` (without `--host`) after the source's GPU resume. If that fails, the source is reported as left suspended and is replaced, since it would read Ready and serve nothing.
- **Record.** The checkpoint's gpushare metadata records `nixl: true`. It also records the pids whose connector the pause released (`nixlPIDs`: every pid addressed but those that answered `ok no ...`). A resume, of the source or of a restore, addresses each of them whether or not the socket scan finds it then, and fails unless each answers `ok`, so a paused process that lost its socket fails the resume rather than stay paused. A checkpoint without `nixlPIDs` resumes the processes with a socket. Only an agent that can resume the connector restores such a checkpoint: its pid-namespace marker is written as `pidns-restore-nixl.json` instead of `pidns-restore.json` (`pidNSMarkerName`, `internal/agent/pidns_capture.go`, chosen before the dump runs). An agent from before `nixl-resume`, after a rollback, finds no marker it reads and refuses the restore before CRIU as a checkpoint it does not restore, so its pod starts cold instead of running an engine whose connector stays paused. Agents with `nixl-resume` read either name; other checkpoints keep the plain name.

## Restore

When the capture paused the connector:

1. Once the restored processes' GPU launches run and the network is unlocked (after `open` and the network unlock for a group, after `resume` otherwise), the agent runs `nixl-resume`.
2. If the restore moved the pod, it passes the pod's own IP as `--host`, which becomes the side channel's address. The IP comes from the restore's address map, else from the API server. If the pod's address can't be read, the restore fails instead of resuming at the captured address, which the pod may not own. Decode engines learn a prefill engine's address per request, so nothing else needs the new IP.
3. The resume runs on the restore's path, before the restore returns. A restore placeholder's readiness waits on the `nvsnap.io/restored` condition, which the agent sets only after the restore returns success (`markRestored`). So the pod does not read Ready, and takes no traffic, while its connector is down. If the resume fails, **the restore fails and the replica starts cold**.

   Two things are checked before CRIU runs, as the hold gate is: that the node's GPU tool has `nixl-resume`, and that the restored pod's address can be read. If either fails, the restore is refused before anything is restored. It counts as a restore that did not run here: not as a restore failure, nor as a stall (three stalls would start the configuration cold for good). The group record counts these refusals apart (`nodeRefusals`), so a node whose bundle lags, or a passing API error, neither blocks a good checkpoint nor ends its restores. A single pod starts cold in place, even one its controller would replace, since a replacement could land on the same node again. In a group, a member refused this way makes the group's restore one that did not run only when every other failed member was aborted for it; a member that failed on its own makes the failure a restore failure. A group's pods are deleted, as after any failure, and their replacements may land on the same node. That is bounded: from the third node refusal, the configuration starts cold for 30 minutes after the last one (its checkpoints kept), then restores again; a restore that runs clears the count.

   The agent disposes of the placeholder, whose engine runs and takes no requests, on every path: a group's leader for its members, the automatic restore for its pod, and the agent itself, in the background after it answers, for a single-pod restore requested through `POST /v1/restore` (the pod is deleted when its controller replaces it, else started cold in place). The restore's marker on the node (`capture_marker.go`) stays until the disposal is done, so an agent that stops before it replaces the pod on its next run.

A restore into another pod also needs the library's UCX route refresh. UCX reads the routing table once per process, and a restored process would otherwise keep the old pod's routes. The library handles UCX 1.22; with another version it logs that UCX keeps the old routes, and `nixl-resume` fails as above.

## Not covered

- SGLang and TRT-LLM;
- NCCL over InfiniBand or RoCE, unless NCCL loads `libnvsnap_ibv.so` (above);
- engines that span nodes;
- ModelExpress and NIXL KV in one pod;
- push-mode connectors and host-buffer KV.

All are refused as before.
